item.title: How to add SEO regression tests to your website's build
item.description: Automated SEO checks that run on every build and pull request: titles, descriptions, canonicals, noindex, schema, sitemaps, headings, and links, with examples.
item.content:encoded:
How to add SEO regression tests to your website's build

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

Most SEO damage on a coded website arrives in an ordinary pull request. Someone refactors a layout, and the canonical tag disappears from 4,000 pages. A content import runs, and every description is blank. Nobody notices for a month, because nobody was looking. A short set of automated checks, run on every build, looks every time. Here is what to test and how to wire it in.

Where the checks run

Continuous integration runs your tests automatically whenever code is pushed. On GitHub Actions, the results appear on the pull request itself, so a reviewer sees a failed check before anyone merges. SEO tests belong in the same place as the unit tests your developers already run: they're just tests whose subject is the built HTML.

The simplest pattern is to build the site, then run a script over the output. A static or prerendered site produces a folder of HTML files to read directly. A server rendered site can be started in the CI job and fetched page by page from a list of representative URLs, one per template.

The checks worth having

Titles and descriptions

  • Every page has exactly one title element and one meta description, and neither is empty.
  • No two pages share a title or a description. Google's documentation asks for distinct titles on every page and warns against repeated or boilerplate text, and it says the same of descriptions.
  • Lengths stay inside a range you choose. Google sets no length limit and truncates to fit the device, so the range is a house style. Mine is 50 to 60 characters for titles and 140 to 160 for descriptions, and the build enforces it.

Indexing signals

  • Every indexable page carries exactly one canonical tag, pointing at its own production URL.
  • No production page carries a noindex, unless it's on an explicit allow list.
  • robots.txt in the production build allows what you expect and lists the sitemap.

Sitemap agreement

  • Every URL in the sitemap exists in the build and returns 200.
  • Every indexable page in the build appears in the sitemap.

Structured data

  • Every JSON-LD block parses as valid JSON.
  • Each template emits the types it should, such as Product on product pages and Article on posts.
  • Key values match the visible page. Google's guidelines say structured data should represent the main content of the page and describe content the user can see, so a price or a name in the JSON-LD that differs from the page is a real fault.

Headings and markup

  • Exactly one H1 per page.
  • The HTML parses with balanced tags and no invalid nesting, which also heads off a class of React hydration errors.

Links

  • Every internal link points at a page that exists in the build.
  • No internal link points at a URL that redirects, so links go straight to the final address.

A minimal example

A check doesn't need a framework. This Python sketch reads every built page and fails the build on a missing or duplicate title:

import pathlib, re, sys
seen, problems = {}, []
for page in pathlib.Path("out").rglob("*.html"):
    html = page.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    titles = re.findall(r"<title>(.*?)</title>", html, re.S)
    if len(titles) != 1:
        problems.append(f"{page}: {len(titles)} title elements")
        continue
    seen.setdefault(titles[0].strip(), []).append(str(page))
for title, pages in seen.items():
    if len(pages) > 1:
        problems.append(f"duplicate title {title!r}: {pages}")
print("\n".join(problems))
sys.exit(1 if problems else 0)

Add a step to the CI workflow that runs it after the build. A nonzero exit fails the check, and the message names the page and the rule, so the developer can fix it without asking anyone. For anything beyond a sketch, use a real HTML parser in place of regular expressions.

Checks that guard the writing, too

Build checks can protect content as well as markup. This site's build compares the text of every page with every other page and fails when two pages share more than 15% of their six word phrases, or when a sentence of ten or more words appears on two pages. That keeps near duplicate pages from creeping in as the site grows. A similar rule suits any site that publishes many pages from a shared template, such as location or category pages.

Rolling it out without blocking everyone

  1. Start in report only mode. Run the checks and print the results without failing the build, and fix the existing backlog.
  2. Turn on failure one rule at a time, starting with the ones that cost the most when they break: canonicals, noindex, and robots.txt.
  3. Keep messages specific. "Missing canonical on /products/blue-widget/" gets fixed in a minute. "SEO check failed" gets the check switched off.
  4. Make the rules a file in the repository, reviewed like code, so changing a threshold is a decision someone signs off.

What tests can't tell you

Build checks prove the HTML you ship meets your rules. They can't tell you how Google ranks it, whether a title persuades anyone to click, or what an AI assistant says about you. Pair them with a crawl of the live site after each release and with Search Console, and keep a person reading the pages.

I write these checks into client repositories as part of SEO engineering. For the Next.js specifics they should cover, see the Next.js SEO checklist, and for safe repository setup, giving an outside SEO access.

  • GitHub Docs: About continuous integration
  • Google Search Central: Influencing your title links
  • Google Search Central: Control your snippets
  • Google Search Central: General structured data guidelines

item.title: How to give an outside SEO safe access to your code repository
item.description: A safe setup for letting an SEO consultant into your GitHub or GitLab repository: one repo, the Read role first, reviewed pull requests, and no secrets.
item.content:encoded:
How to give an outside SEO safe access to your code repository

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

On a site built with Next.js, React, or a headless CMS, the search problems live in the code, so the person fixing them needs to see it. Granting that access is a small, routine job when you set it up in the right order. Here is the order I ask clients to follow, and the reasons behind each step.

Why an SEO asks for the repository at all

A crawl tells me that 900 pages share a title. The repository tells me which component writes it, which data it reads, and whether a fix will reach every route that uses it. Without the code, I write a ticket describing the symptom and your developer goes looking for the cause. With it, the ticket names the file, or arrives as a pull request ready for review. Read access alone usually cuts the time from finding to fix by a wide margin.

Invite them to one repository, as an outside collaborator

On GitHub, a consultant belongs outside your organization's membership. Add them as an outside collaborator on the one repository that builds the website, rather than as an organization member who inherits base permissions across everything you own. Your other repositories, your internal tools, and your infrastructure code stay out of view. If the site is split across a frontend and a content repository, add them to both and nothing else.

Start with the Read role

GitHub's repository roles, from least access to most, are Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, and Admin. GitHub's own guidance is to pick the role that fits each person's function without giving them more access than they need.

  • Read is GitHub's role for people who view or discuss a project without changing it. That covers the whole diagnostic phase.
  • Triage adds managing issues and pull requests without write access, which suits a consultant who files tickets in your tracker.
  • Write is for contributors who push to the project, which an SEO needs only once they start making changes themselves.
  • Maintain and Admin are for your own team. An outside SEO never needs either.

GitLab has its own set: Guest, Reporter, Developer, Maintainer, and Owner, ordered from fewest permissions to most, plus specialized Planner and Security Manager roles. Reporter is the usual starting point for an outside reviewer there, and Developer is roughly the equivalent of GitHub's Write.

Grant Write only after main is protected

Before anyone outside your team can push, make sure nobody can push straight to your main branch. On GitHub, a ruleset or a branch protection rule controls who can push to a branch and can require reviews on pull requests before they merge. GitHub's documentation notes that when both a ruleset and a protection rule apply to the same branch, all the rules apply, and the most restrictive version of each wins.

With that in place, Write access becomes safe: the consultant can create branches and open pull requests, and every change still waits for one of your people to approve it. Nothing they write reaches production without your review.

Use deploy previews to see each change before merge

Netlify builds a Deploy Preview for pull requests in a connected GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps repository, and Vercel creates a preview deployment for every push to a non-production branch and every pull request. Each preview gets its own URL. Your team can click through the change, and I can check what a crawler will see on it: titles, canonicals, structured data, status codes, and rendered content. Netlify adds an X-Robots-Tag: noindex header to its previews, which asks search engines to leave them out of results. For anything sensitive, Netlify recommends password protection on top.

Keep secrets out of the repository

API keys, database passwords, and tokens belong in your host's environment variables, never in a committed file. Anyone you give read access can read every file and its history, so a key committed two years ago and deleted since is still visible to them. Two habits protect you:

  • Turn on push protection. GitHub's push protection is a secret scanning feature that blocks pushes containing recognized credentials before they reach the repository, from the command line, the web interface, and the API.
  • Rotate anything that ever leaked. If secret scanning finds an old key in the history, revoke it and issue a new one before you invite anyone in.

An SEO needs no production credentials to do this work. If someone asks for them, ask why.

The CMS only option

Some teams can't open the codebase, for contractual or security reasons. That still leaves plenty of room. Give the consultant an editor role in the CMS for content, titles, and descriptions, Search Console access, and the preview URLs. They write tickets with the evidence and the acceptance criteria, and your developer makes the code changes. It's slower, and it works.

Remove access when the engagement ends

Put the end date in your own calendar on the day you grant access. When the work finishes, remove the outside collaborator from the repository, take them out of Search Console and the hosting dashboard, and revoke any deploy keys or tokens created for the engagement.

A checklist for the day you say yes

  1. Invite the consultant as an outside collaborator on the website repository only.
  2. Assign Read on GitHub, or Reporter on GitLab.
  3. Confirm deploy previews are switched on for pull requests.
  4. Check that push protection or secret scanning is enabled and the history is clean.
  5. Add a ruleset or branch protection requiring a reviewed pull request on main.
  6. Move to Write, or Developer, only once that rule is in place.
  7. Set a reminder to remove every grant at the end date.

This is the setup I ask for at the start of an SEO engineering engagement. For how I work once I'm in, see developer specs and QA and the guide to working safely with AI coding assistants.

References

  • GitHub Docs: About rulesets
  • GitHub Docs: About push protection
  • GitLab Docs: Roles and permissions
  • Netlify Docs: Deploy Previews
  • Vercel Docs: Preview deployments

item.title: A Next.js SEO checklist for the App Router
item.description: A Next.js App Router SEO checklist: metadata, canonicals, title templates, streamed metadata, sitemap.ts, robots.ts, 308 redirects, real 404s, and schema.
item.content:encoded:
A Next.js SEO checklist for the App Router

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

Next.js gives you everything a search engine needs, as code: metadata, sitemaps, robots rules, redirects, and status codes. Every one of them can also be left at a default that quietly hurts you. This is the list I work through on every Next.js site, in the order I check it.

1. Every route sets its own title and description

In the App Router, metadata comes from a metadata object or a generateMetadata function exported from a layout or page. Static pages can use the object. Pages built from data, such as products, posts, and locations, need generateMetadata so each URL gets its own title and description from its own record.

Both exports work only in Server Components, which keeps the tags in the server's HTML. If a page needs client side features, keep page.tsx as a Server Component and move the interactive parts into a child component.

2. The title template does what you meant

A title.template in the root layout, such as '%s | Brand', adds a suffix to every child page's title, and title.default fills in for pages that set none. That's convenient, and it's also how a site ends up with 2,000 pages titled with the brand name alone. Crawl the site and sort titles by frequency: any title used more than a few times is a page that fell through to the default.

3. Canonicals are set per route, with a metadataBase

Set metadataBase once in the root layout, then give each route alternates.canonical. Next.js combines the two into a full URL. Check the output on routes with query strings and on paginated lists, where a template canonical copied from the parent layout can point every page at page one.

4. You know what crawlers receive when metadata streams

When generateMetadata waits on request time data, Next.js can stream the page first and append the metadata tags to the body once they resolve. It does that for crawlers it expects to run JavaScript, such as Googlebot, and blocks rendering to put the tags in the head for a list of HTML limited bots, including Bingbot, social preview bots, and several others. GPTBot, ClaudeBot, and PerplexityBot are absent from the default list in the Next.js source. If AI crawler visibility matters to you, fetch your key pages with those user agents and check where the title and canonical land. The htmlLimitedBots option in the Next.js config lets you add them, at some cost in response time.

5. The sitemap is generated, complete, and honest

An app/sitemap.ts file that returns an array of URLs produces /sitemap.xml. Generate it from the same data source as the routes, include only canonical, indexable URLs that return 200, and set lastModified from the content's real update date rather than the build time. Large sites can split into several sitemaps. Compare the sitemap with a crawl: every URL in one should be in the other.

6. robots.ts says what you mean, for each crawler

An app/robots.ts file generates /robots.txt, with rules per user agent and a sitemap line. Decide deliberately about AI crawlers, and make sure preview and staging deployments disallow everything while production allows what you intend. A single environment variable deciding which robots file ships is a common source of a production site that tells every crawler to stay out.

7. Redirects are permanent where you mean permanent

Redirects in next.config.js take a source, a destination, and a permanent flag. With permanent: true Next.js returns a 308, the permanent status that tells browsers and search engines to remember the move. With false it returns a 307, a temporary redirect that nothing caches. A migration map written with permanent: false tells search engines to keep the old URLs. Check every rule's flag, and test the map against a crawl of the old site.

8. Missing pages return a real 404

Calling notFound() renders the not-found page, returns a 404, and adds a noindex tag. One catch: if the check runs inside a Suspense boundary after the response has started streaming, the status is already sent, so the page keeps its 200 and relies on the noindex tag. Run the existence check before streaming begins on routes where a real 404 matters, such as products and posts that get deleted. Then crawl a list of deliberately broken URLs and confirm the status codes.

9. JSON-LD is rendered in the component

The Next.js recommendation is a plain <script type="application/ld+json"> in the layout or page, built from the same data as the visible content. Escape the < character in the JSON, as the Next.js guide shows, so content from a CMS can't inject script. Validate a sample from each template with the Rich Results Test or the Schema Markup Validator.

10. Navigation uses real links

The Link component extends the HTML anchor element, so it produces an <a href> that crawlers can follow. Navigation built from buttons with router.push in a click handler produces no link at all. Search the codebase for click handlers that navigate, and crawl with JavaScript rendering off to see which pages are reachable from plain HTML.

11. The rendered page matches the server page

Finally, compare the raw HTML with the rendered DOM on each template, and run the pages in headless Chrome to collect console errors. Hydration mismatches, content that loads only after interaction, and client side redirects all show up here. The guide to React hydration errors covers the most common fault.

Make the checklist permanent

Every item above can become an automated check in the build, so a future change can't undo it. That's the subject of adding SEO tests to your website's build.

I work through this list, and fix what it finds, as part of SEO engineering for Next.js and React sites. If you're bringing me into your repository, start with how to give an outside SEO safe access.

References

  • Next.js: robots.txt
  • Next.js: redirects
  • Next.js: notFound
  • Next.js: JSON-LD
  • Next.js: Link component

item.title: The SEO tools for a website migration, and the job each one does
item.description: The tools that carry a website migration safely: crawlers, Search Console, redirect testing, crawl comparison, and analytics, with the job each one does.
item.content:encoded:
The SEO tools for a website migration, and the job each one does

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

No single product migrates a website for you. A migration is a handful of jobs, and each has a tool that does it well: an inventory, a redirect map, a pre-launch comparison, a launch day test, and weeks of watching. Here is the kit I use, matched to the job, with the free options where they exist.

Job 1: list every URL that matters

The inventory is the foundation, and it comes from several tools at once, since no single source sees everything.

  • A crawler. Screaming Frog SEO Spider, Sitebulb, or a similar desktop crawler finds every URL linked from the site. Screaming Frog's free version stops at 500 URLs; a licence removes the limit.
  • Google Search Console. The Performance report, exported by page over the last twelve to sixteen months, lists the URLs that actually earn impressions, including ones no longer linked from anywhere.
  • Analytics. Landing pages from GA4 or whatever you run, for the URLs people arrive on from every channel.
  • A backlink tool. Ahrefs, Semrush, or Majestic for the URLs other sites link to, which carry value even if they earn no traffic.
  • The XML sitemaps and, if you can get them, server logs.

Merge them into one spreadsheet with a row per URL and columns for clicks, links, and sessions. That's the list everything else is tested against.

Job 2: build and store the redirect map

The map pairs each old URL with its closest new equivalent. A spreadsheet is fine for drafting. The finished map belongs wherever the new site serves redirects: the server configuration, the host's redirect rules file on Netlify, Vercel, or Cloudflare, or the framework's own configuration. In Next.js, for example, redirects live in next.config.js, and each rule's permanent flag decides between a 308 and a 307. Keeping the map in version control means it gets reviewed, and nobody loses it.

For large sites, pattern rules cover whole sections in one line, and exceptions handle the pages that don't fit the pattern. Test the patterns before launch, because one bad regex can redirect thousands of pages to the wrong place.

Job 3: compare staging with the live site

Before launch, crawl both the live site and the staging site with the same settings, then compare them. Screaming Frog's crawl comparison does this with URL Mapping, which uses a regex to pair the staging hostname's URLs with the live ones. You see, template by template, which titles, descriptions, headings, canonicals, structured data, and internal links changed. It needs a licence and database storage mode.

Check the staging site's robots.txt and meta robots tags at the same time. Staging is supposed to be blocked from search. Production isn't, and the block coming across at launch is one of the most common migration disasters.

Job 4: test every redirect on launch day

Once the redirects are live, crawl the old URL list in Screaming Frog's list mode with Always Follow Redirects switched on, as Screaming Frog's migration guide describes. The All Redirects report shows each old URL, where it finally lands, and every hop in between, so you can spot 404s, chains, loops, and temporary redirects in minutes. Run it again a day later, after caches have cleared.

For a quick spot check without a crawler, curl -sI on the command line shows the status code and the Location header for any single URL.

Job 5: tell Google, then watch

  • Search Console sitemaps. Google's site move guidance is to submit the sitemaps for both the old and new URLs, then watch the indexed count move from one to the other. Warnings that the old URLs redirect are expected.
  • The Change of Address tool, for moves from one domain or subdomain to another, used after the redirects are in place. It doesn't apply to HTTP to HTTPS, www changes, or path changes within one site.
  • URL Inspection, on a sample of important old and new URLs, to see Google's chosen canonical and indexing status.
  • The Performance report with a date comparison, by page, to catch any section that loses more than the expected dip.
  • Bing Webmaster Tools, the equivalent for Bing, which also supplies results to other search and AI products.
  • Server logs, which Google also recommends checking during a move, to confirm Googlebot is crawling the new URLs and to catch error codes your crawler missed.

Job 6: prove the move held

A few weeks after launch, crawl the new site again and compare it with the pre-launch staging crawl, and rerun the old URL list. Anything that drifted, such as a redirect someone edited or a template change that dropped schema, shows up as a difference. If the numbers have fallen and stayed down, the migration recovery guide covers what to do next.

What a tool can't do

Every tool above reports facts. None of them decides which new page is the right home for an old one, whether a thin page should be merged or kept, or which redirect rule is safe on a site with forty thousand URLs. That judgment is the migration work itself, and it's why the inventory and the map deserve the most time.

I run migrations with this kit as website migration SEO. For the full sequence, follow the website migration checklist, and for redirect rules in depth, see 301 redirects explained.

  • Search Console Help: Change of Address tool

  • Next.js: redirects

item.title: Traffic fell after a site migration: how to find what broke and get it back
item.description: A recovery plan for a website migration that lost search traffic: rebuild the old URL list, test every redirect, compare old and new pages, and fix in order.
item.content:encoded:
Traffic fell after a site migration: how to find what broke and get it back

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

The new site launched, and organic traffic dropped and stayed down. Some dip is normal while Google recrawls. A drop that's still there after a month has a cause, and it's almost always one of a short list. Here is the recovery routine I run, in the order that finds the money fastest.

First, separate normal turbulence from real loss

Google says to expect ranking fluctuations during any significant move, and that for a medium sized site it can take a few weeks or more before the new URLs gradually replace the old ones in results, longer for large sites. So the first question is shape. A dip that's recovering week over week is the move settling. A cliff that hasn't moved, or losses concentrated in one section, is a fault.

In Search Console, compare the four weeks after launch with the four weeks before, and look at pages rather than totals. Sort by lost clicks. The top twenty URLs usually account for most of the loss, and they tell you where to dig.

Rebuild the list of old URLs

Every recovery starts with the URL inventory the migration should have started with. If nobody kept one, rebuild it from every source you can reach:

  • The Search Console Performance report for the months before launch, exported by page.
  • Analytics landing pages for the same period.
  • The old XML sitemaps, from a backup or from the Wayback Machine.
  • A backlink tool's list of linked URLs on your domain.
  • Server logs, if the old host kept them.

Merge them and remove duplicates. This list, weighted by the traffic and links each URL carried, is what you'll test.

Test every old URL's redirect

Screaming Frog's own migration guide describes the method. Switch to list mode, turn on Always Follow Redirects under Config > Spider > Advanced, upload the old URLs, and crawl them. The All Redirects export then shows each old address, the final address it lands on, the type of each hop, and whether a chain or a loop is involved.

Read the export for these failures, in this order:

  1. 404s and soft 404s. Old URLs with no redirect at all. On a big site these are usually whole patterns, such as an old category path or a dropped file extension.
  2. Redirects to the home page or a generic category. Google treats a redirect to an unrelated page much like a missing page, and the old URL's value doesn't carry over.
  3. Temporary redirects. Google's documentation says a permanent redirect shows the new target in results, while a temporary one keeps showing the source. A migration built on 302s or 307s is telling Google to keep the old URLs.
  4. Chains and loops. Each extra hop slows crawling, and loops never resolve.
  5. JavaScript and meta refresh redirects. Google ranks server side redirects as the most reliable way to signal a move. Anything else should be replaced with one.

Compare old pages with their new versions

A redirect that lands on the right URL still loses traffic if the new page is weaker. If you have a crawl from before launch, compare it with a crawl of the new site in Screaming Frog's comparison mode, using URL Mapping to pair old and new addresses. Without one, archived copies of the top pages will do. Check each pair for:

  • Titles, descriptions, and H1s that were rewritten, shortened, or replaced with a template default.
  • Body copy cut down, split across tabs, or moved behind a script.
  • Structured data that existed before and doesn't now.
  • Internal links that used to point at the page and no longer do, which shows up as greater crawl depth.
  • Canonical tags pointing at staging, at the old domain, or at the wrong page.
  • A noindex or a robots.txt rule carried over from the staging site.

Check that Google can see the new site the way you think

Use URL Inspection on a sample of the top lost URLs and their new equivalents. Look at Google's chosen canonical, the indexing status, and the rendered page. Check the old sitemap and the new one in the Sitemaps report: Google's guidance is to submit both during a move, and to expect the indexed count on the old one to fall as the new one rises. If the old URLs still show as indexed weeks later, Google isn't following your redirects as you intended.

For a move to a new domain, confirm the Change of Address request went in from the old property. Google's help is specific about when it applies: a move between domains or subdomains. HTTP to HTTPS, www to non-www, and path changes within one site don't use it.

Fix in order of value

Recovery work goes fastest when it follows the money. Fix the redirects for the twenty URLs that lost the most first, then the patterns that cover hundreds of URLs at once, then content and template gaps on the pages that matter, then the long tail. Keep every redirect in place: Google recommends at least a year, and longer is better for people following old links.

After each round of fixes, run the list crawl again and confirm the failures are gone, then watch the affected pages in Search Console. Recovered pages usually come back over weeks, as Google recrawls them. I make no promise about full recovery, because rankings also move for reasons unrelated to the migration, but a site whose old URLs all resolve cleanly to equal or better pages has removed every cause it controls.

Keep the evidence

Write down what you found, what you fixed, and when, with the before and after crawl exports. If traffic doesn't come back in the expected window, that record is what lets the next person separate a migration fault from an algorithm update or a seasonal dip.

I handle this as part of website migration SEO, and for inherited projects that went badly, project rescue. To prevent the next one, use the website migration checklist and the tools I use for a website migration.

item.title: React hydration errors and what they mean for SEO
item.description: What React error 418 and other hydration mismatches are, why Google usually still indexes the page, what they cost in speed and analytics, and how to find them.
item.content:encoded:
React hydration errors and what they mean for SEO

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

If your browser console on a React or Next.js site shows "Minified React error #418," the page has a hydration error. It rarely stops Google from indexing the content, so it's easy to leave alone. It still costs you layout stability, responsiveness, and trustworthy analytics, and it usually points at a markup fault worth fixing at the source.

What hydration is

A server rendered React page arrives as finished HTML, so visitors and crawlers see content immediately. Then React loads in the browser and "attaches" itself to that HTML, wiring up buttons, menus, and forms. React calls this hydration: it turns the server's HTML snapshot into an interactive app.

For that to work, the HTML React expects to find has to match what the server sent. React's documentation says it expects the rendered content to be identical, and that you should treat mismatches as bugs and fix them.

What error #418 means

Production builds of React strip long error messages to save bytes and print a number instead. React's error page decodes #418 as: hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client, and as a result the tree will be regenerated on the client. In plain terms, React gave up on the server's HTML for that part of the page and built it again in the browser.

What it means for search

Google crawls the server's response first, and server rendering means the content is already in that HTML. Google's JavaScript SEO documentation still recommends server side or pre-rendering for exactly that reason: it's faster for users and crawlers, and not every bot runs JavaScript. A hydration error happens after that HTML is delivered, so the words on the page usually still reach the index.

The costs show up elsewhere:

  • Layout shift. When React throws away server markup and re-renders, elements can jump, which counts against Cumulative Layout Shift.
  • Slower interaction. Rebuilding part of the page on the main thread can delay the response to the visitor's first tap or click, which shows up in Interaction to Next Paint.
  • Broken widgets. Components in the rebuilt section lose whatever state they had, so a menu, carousel, or form can reset or stop responding.
  • Messy analytics. Tags that fire on load can fire twice, or against elements that have since been replaced.

Head tags are a separate concern. In Next.js, metadata set with generateMetadata or a metadata export is resolved on the server and sent as HTML, so titles and canonicals don't depend on hydration succeeding.

The usual causes

React's own list covers most of what I find on real sites:

  • Invalid nesting. A div inside a p, or a link inside a link. The browser's HTML parser rearranges invalid nesting as it reads the page, so the DOM no longer matches the tree React rendered on the server.
  • Unbalanced HTML from a CMS. Rich text injected with dangerouslySetInnerHTML that contains a stray closing tag or an unclosed element. The browser repairs it on the way in, and React finds a different structure from the one it expected.
  • Dates and locales. A date formatted on the server in one time zone or locale and on the client in another.
  • Random values. IDs or keys generated with Math.random() or Date.now(), which differ between the two renders.
  • Browser checks during render. A branch like typeof window !== 'undefined' that renders one thing on the server and another in the browser.
  • Browser extensions. Extensions that edit the page before React loads. These show up only for some visitors and aren't yours to fix, which is why it's worth reproducing in a clean browser profile first.

Finding them across a whole site

The browser console shows you one page at a time, and hydration errors often live on a handful of templates or on pages whose CMS content happens to contain bad markup. Spot checking misses them. I script headless Chrome with Playwright to load every URL in the sitemap or the crawl, collect each console error with the URL it came from, and group the results by template. A few hundred pages run in minutes.

The production build tells you only that a mismatch happened. To see where, run the same page against a development build, where React warns about each mismatch with its full message instead of a number. Once the list is grouped, the cause for each template is usually obvious within a few minutes of reading.

Fixing them at the source

  • Correct the nesting in the component, using a div or span where a paragraph can't legally contain the child.
  • Repair the content that carries unbalanced HTML, and sanitize rich text on the way into the CMS or at render time.
  • Make server and client agree on dates by fixing the time zone and locale, and generate IDs with React's useId rather than random numbers.
  • Move browser only logic into an effect that runs after hydration.
  • Silence only the unavoidable. React offers suppressHydrationWarning for a single element whose text must differ, such as a timestamp. Use it on that element and nowhere else.

Then stop the problem coming back. A small check in the build that parses every rendered page and fails on unbalanced tags or invalid nesting catches the CMS content that would have caused the next one.

item.description: A claim by claim method for checking polished AI answers about SEO, using a real exchange about brand names in page titles and what the evidence supports.
item.content:encoded:
How to fact check a confident AI answer about SEO before you act on it

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

I asked an AI search assistant whether ending every page title with a pipe and the company name hurts a website. The answer came back polished, cited, and full of percentages. When I pushed my own opinion back at it, it declared that opinion “100% true” and invented psychology to support it. The recommendation itself was reasonable. A good share of the evidence was not. This is the routine I use to separate the two before anything reaches a client's site.

Turn the answer into a list of claims

Paste the answer into a document and give every sentence that asserts a fact its own line. In this exchange the list read: titles are cut off after about 60 characters; Google rewrites more than 75 percent of titles; Google strips pipes and brand names; Google displays the site name on its own; repeated suffixes cause duplication penalties and dilute relevance; searchers read a pipe as a sign of automated spam.

A sound recommendation can rest on claims that are half wrong. Grading each line separately stops a good conclusion from carrying bad evidence into your report.

Grade every claim by where it comes from

Each line goes into one of four bins: the platform's own documentation, an independent study with a published method, a vendor test, or nothing traceable. Here is how this exchange graded out.

ClaimWhat I found
Titles are cut off at about 60 charactersGoogle's documentation sets no maximum length and says the displayed title is shortened to fit the device. Sixty characters is an industry habit, not a Google limit.
Google rewrites over 75 percent of titlesI could not trace that figure to a primary dataset about pipes or brand names. The best documented study I found, by Zyppy, measured 61.6 percent of 80,959 titles on 2,370 sites, using desktop results from early 2022. Titles longer than 70 characters were rewritten 99.9 percent of the time.
Google strips pipesThe same study found pipes removed or replaced in 41.0 percent of titles that used them, often swapped for a dash. Dashes were removed 19.7 percent of the time.
Google strips brand namesThe study names missing or superfluous brand names as a rewrite trigger and gives no percentage. Google says it may omit a site name that repeats the one already shown.
Google shows the site name separatelySupported by Google's documentation.
Repeated suffixes cause penalties or crawling problemsNothing traceable. Google warns that boilerplate titles make results hard to tell apart, which is about usefulness to searchers, not a penalty.
Searchers read a pipe as spamNothing traceable. I found no study measuring that reaction.

Follow every number back to its population

A statistic describes the set of things someone counted, at a particular time, in a particular way. Ask who measured it, when, on which device, and what exactly was counted. A rewrite rate for all titles says nothing specific about pipes. A desktop sample from early 2022 may not describe mobile results today. When an assistant cannot show where a number came from, or the source measures something else, drop the number and keep the point in plain words.

Distrust agreement that grows when you push

The clearest warning in this exchange came after I shared my own view. The follow-up adopted my wording, raised its certainty, and added mechanisms nobody had measured. An assistant that grows more confident because you sounded confident is reflecting you back at yourself. Open a fresh conversation and ask the opposite question: what is the case for keeping the company name in every title? If the answer flips that easily, the evidence was never doing the work.

Settle it with your own data

For title changes, the deciding evidence sits in your own Search Console. Change one group of pages, leave a comparable group untouched, and compare clicks and click-through rate across several weeks. A controlled result from your own site outranks any general statistic, accurate or invented. My guide to diagnosing a Google traffic drop in Search Console covers lining changes up with dates, and the one on measuring AI citations, referrals, and leads applies the same discipline to AI search reporting.

What survived the check

After grading, the defensible advice fit in a few lines: write a specific title for each page, include the company name where it helps someone recognize or choose the result, keep titles concise, and measure the change. Dropping a repeated suffix remains a legitimate editorial call. It simply has to be presented as judgment backed by a test, never as escape from a penalty that does not exist.

item.title: Diagnosing Core Web Vitals with MCP and an AI coding assistant
item.description: How to diagnose LCP, INP, and CLS with an AI coding assistant through MCP: Chrome DevTools traces, real user CrUX data, and Screaming Frog at scale.
item.content:encoded:
Diagnosing Core Web Vitals with MCP and an AI coding assistant

By Chris Abraham · Published October 13, 2026

Fixing a slow page used to mean running a test, reading a waterfall, opening the code, and going back and forth between the three. With the Model Context Protocol, an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code can drive Chrome, record a performance trace, read the result, and open the component responsible, all in one session. Here is how I set it up, what each piece does, and where a person still has to check the work.

The three numbers you're chasing

Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Google's web.dev thresholds for a good experience are a Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and a Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads on mobile and desktop separately. A page passes when it meets all three. The Core Web Vitals guide explains each metric and its usual causes; this guide is about the tooling.

What MCP adds

MCP is a standard way for an AI assistant to call outside tools. An MCP server wraps a tool, such as a browser or a crawler, and the assistant can ask it to do things and read back the results. In Claude Code, you register a server with claude mcp add, and its tools become available in the session. The assistant still needs you to tell it what to look at and to check its conclusions, but the tedious loop of test, read, and search the code collapses into one conversation.

Chrome DevTools MCP: lab traces on demand

Google's Chrome DevTools MCP server gives an assistant control of a real Chrome browser and the DevTools performance panel. Its documented setup for Claude Code is a single command:

claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest

The tools that matter for Core Web Vitals:

  • performance_start_trace and performance_stop_trace record a trace, optionally reloading the page and bypassing the cache to measure a cold load. The tool is described as finding frontend performance issues and Core Web Vitals.
  • performance_analyze_insight opens a specific finding from the trace, such as the LCP breakdown, which shows where the time before the largest element appeared actually went.
  • emulate throttles the CPU and network, with presets from Slow 3G to Fast 4G, and sets a mobile viewport, so a fast desktop doesn't hide a slow phone experience.
  • list_console_messages and list_network_requests show errors and the heaviest resources.
  • lighthouse_audit runs Lighthouse for accessibility, SEO, and best practices. Its documentation notes that it excludes performance, which is what the trace tools are for.

Two settings are worth knowing. The performance tools can send the traced URL to Google's CrUX API to show real user data beside the lab result; the --no-performance-crux flag turns that off. And Google collects usage statistics from the server by default, which --no-usage-statistics disables.

Real user data: CrUX, and a change to PageSpeed Insights

A lab trace shows one load on one machine. Search uses field data from real Chrome users, collected in the Chrome UX Report. The CrUX API returns that data for a page or a whole origin, with a Google Cloud API key set up for it.

One change to plan around: Google's PageSpeed Insights API documentation says Google plans to stop including CrUX real user data in that API, and recommends the CrUX API or the CrUX History API instead. Any script or dashboard that pulls field data from PageSpeed Insights should move now.

Screaming Frog: every template, not one page

Traces are for depth. For breadth, Screaming Frog's PageSpeed Insights integration, under Configuration > API Access > PageSpeed Insights, pulls Lighthouse metrics and opportunities for every URL during a crawl. It can also run Lighthouse locally, which avoids the API's daily query limit but has no CrUX data.

Screaming Frog version 24 also runs as an MCP server, so an assistant can start crawls and read reports and bulk exports directly. It's a paid licence feature and needs database storage mode. Optional tools let the assistant run Node.js scripts, and they're off until you enable them in the MCP server settings.

The combination is where the time savings live: crawl every URL, group the slow ones by template, trace one representative page per template, and fix the template once.

A working session, step by step

  1. Start from field data. Check the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console or the CrUX API to see which metric fails and on which group of pages.
  2. Pick representative URLs, one per failing template.
  3. Trace each on emulated mobile. Ask the assistant to throttle to a mid-range phone and record a cold load.
  4. Read the insight, then the code. For a slow LCP, the breakdown shows whether the time goes to the server, to fetching the hero image, or to rendering. With the repository open, the assistant can find the component that loads the image and propose a change, such as preloading it or removing its lazy loading.
  5. Test on a preview. Trace the same page on the branch's preview deployment and compare.
  6. Confirm in the field. CrUX data is a rolling 28 day window, so real user numbers improve gradually after release.

Where to keep a hand on the wheel

  • Lab is not field. A trace on a developer's machine, even throttled, is one sample. Treat it as a diagnosis and judge the outcome by field data.
  • Check every proposed fix. An assistant can suggest deferring a script that the page needs, or a preload that competes with the real LCP image. Measure before and after.
  • Mind what the browser can see. The DevTools server's own documentation warns that it exposes the browser's content to the assistant. Use a separate browser profile, never one signed in to anything sensitive.
  • INP needs interaction. A page load trace says little about responsiveness. Have the assistant click, type, and open menus during a trace, and compare with field INP.

This is how I run speed work on code based sites as part of site speed and Core Web Vitals and SEO engineering. For the habits that keep an AI assistant safe in a client codebase, see using AI coding assistants on a business website.

item.title: How to measure AI search citations, referrals, and actual leads
item.description: Build an honest AI search report that separates citations, referral visits, and leads using Bing Webmaster Tools, GA4, repeatable checks, and clear limits.
item.content:encoded:
How to measure AI search citations, referrals, and actual leads

By Chris Abraham · Published October 12, 2026

An AI answer mentions your business. Someone sends a screenshot. Another person asks whether revenue has increased. Those are three different observations, and a useful report keeps them separate. I would build a small measurement routine around citations, identifiable visits, and business outcomes, with a note explaining what each source can and cannot see.

Define the outcome before choosing a dashboard

A citation is a reference to a page in an answer. A mention names the business and might provide no link. A referral is a visit with an identifiable source. A lead is a business event, such as an inquiry or completed booking. None of those measures is interchangeable with the others.

Choose the question the report needs to answer. If the goal is correcting inaccurate descriptions, an answer log may be the best instrument. If the goal is qualified inquiries, analytics and the inquiry record matter more. If the goal is finding which articles become sources, provider citation reporting deserves attention.

I would avoid combining these into an invented visibility score. A score can hide a rise in mentions alongside a fall in meaningful visits. Show the underlying observations and let the reader understand the tradeoffs.

Read Bing's citation reporting within its boundaries

Bing Webmaster Tools provides an AI Performance report for Microsoft Copilot, Bing, and selected partner experiences. Microsoft's June 2026 update added preview capabilities for intent, topic, citation share, and period comparisons. These are provider observations, not a census of every AI product.

Review the cited pages and the retrieval queries associated with them. A grounding query reflects the system's search for supporting material; do not present it as a verbatim customer question. Topic and intent groupings can suggest editorial questions worth investigating, but their labels are not a substitute for reading the actual pages.

Microsoft defines citation share around the citations for a particular grounding query. It is not traffic share or a content quality score. When reporting a change, retain the dates and scope of the comparison. A movement may reflect demand, system changes, or other sources as well as your own revisions.

Build a separate view of identifiable visits

In GA4, examine session source and medium alongside the landing page. Start with the referring domains that actually appear in your own data rather than copying an enormous list from a marketing article. Check whether visits from an assistant are being grouped with referrals or another channel.

Google Analytics lets a property use custom channel groups while leaving its default channel definitions intact. A custom group can make recognized AI referrals easier to review. Document the matching rules and check for overlap with existing categories before using the group in a recurring report.

Source information is incomplete. Apps, browser privacy settings, and links that do not pass a referrer can obscure where a visit began. A visit without source information is not automatically an AI visit. Report the identifiable portion as such, and resist estimating the rest from a guess.

For links you control in a campaign, consistent tagging can help attribution. You cannot assume that an assistant will preserve tags or that every visitor will follow the cited link. Keep citation totals and session totals in separate columns.

Keep Google's reporting distinct

Google documents traffic from its AI search features within the Search Console Performance report's Web search type. That aggregate is not a dedicated citation inventory. Do not label a change in all Google impressions as a measured change in AI citations.

Use page and query comparisons to locate changes in search performance, then investigate them. A title revision, a changed canonical, seasonality, or an indexing issue may matter. A chart moving after a publishing change establishes timing; it does not prove the change caused the movement.

Create a repeatable answer log

A manual check is useful when its conditions are saved. Choose a short list of genuine customer questions and preserve the exact wording. Record the product, mode, date, relevant account or location context, answer summary, cited addresses, and factual inaccuracies.

Repeat the same questions on a schedule, with a consistent procedure. If you change the prompt halfway through, label that as a new test. Keep unexpected or unfavorable answers in the record rather than retaining only flattering screenshots.

A practical observation log might contain these fields:

  • Question identifier: a stable label linked to the saved wording.
  • Experience tested: the provider and the relevant search mode.
  • Observed answer: the claim being checked and whether it is accurate.
  • Source addresses: the pages actually linked in that response.
  • Follow up: the correction, page improvement, or further test required.

This is a sample of answers under recorded conditions. It cannot establish your universal position across all users, prompts, and products. The purpose is to detect patterns and factual problems you can act on.

Connect the observations to inquiries

Define a small set of meaningful business events. A contact submission may count; a button click alone may not. Test that the event fires when the action succeeds, and check whether duplicate events inflate the count. Compare the analytics record with actual received inquiries before presenting a conversion total.

An optional “How did you hear about this business?” field can add context, but self reported answers have their own limits. A customer may recall an assistant while the final visit came through a branded search. Preserve both observations without forcing them into one source label.

A hypothetical monthly report could list cited pages, identifiable assistant referrals, qualified inquiries from those visits, and unresolved attribution questions. Keep small counts visible. One additional lead can produce a dramatic percentage change when the previous total was tiny.

Review the evidence before commissioning more content

Ask which pages are repeatedly useful, which questions remain unanswered, and whether the cited explanation is accurate. Improve a specific weakness and record the release date. Compare an appropriate later period, while acknowledging other changes that occurred during it.

The report should end with a decision: repair a factual error, improve a relevant article, investigate tracking, or leave a useful page alone. For the publication side of that process, use the IndexNow and AI search release workflow. If the tracking itself needs work, see analytics setup and repair.

item.content:encoded:
IndexNow, Bing, and a practical AI search workflow for fall 2026

By Chris Abraham · Published October 12, 2026

A website can publish excellent advice and still have a poor release process. The repository changes, the build finishes, a notification runs, and nobody checks which version reached the public domain. My priority for AI search this fall is making that chain observable. Give each release a clear destination, verify the content there, and keep evidence of what happened afterward.

Assign a separate job to each part of the system

A sitemap describes the site's intended public inventory. Internal links give visitors and crawlers routes through it. An RSS feed distributes articles to subscribers and other publishing systems. IndexNow sends change notifications to participating engines. None of these substitutes for a page that explains something accurately.

The distinctions matter when a stakeholder asks whether a guide has been “submitted to AI.” There is no single submission step that covers every assistant. Search products can retrieve information through different providers and their own crawlers. IndexNow can support freshness in participating indexes, but it is not a pipeline into every language model.

I would name the checkpoints in a release record: committed, built, deployed, publicly verified, notified, crawled, and indexed. A citation is another observation, not a synonym for any of those states. That vocabulary prevents a green build badge from becoming an unsupported visibility claim.

Prepare the page before setting up notifications

Choose a permanent address and connect it to the right guide category. Confirm the title describes the question, the introduction supplies an answer, and the author's identity is clear. Check the visible content against the structured data. If a comparison uses numbers, publish the assumptions and the date of the comparison.

Then request the public address directly. It should return the expected page without requiring an editor session. Inspect the canonical and indexing controls, and test important images and downloadable resources. Compare the raw HTML with the rendered page when JavaScript is involved. My JavaScript visibility guide provides a focused diagnostic sequence.

Google's AI search documentation keeps the eligibility requirements within ordinary Search: the page must be indexed and allowed to appear with a snippet. Extra AI specific markup is not required. I would spend the first hour correcting access or content problems before adding another machine readable file.

Make IndexNow part of the release process

The protocol verifies control of a host through a key file. Publish that file where the submitted key location points, and confirm its contents from the public domain. Submit the final URLs on that host, rather than preview addresses or a development domain. Preserve the verification file through template changes and migrations.

Send notifications for meaningful additions, revisions, or removals. The documentation permits batches of up to 10,000 URLs, but a normal editorial release rarely needs that many. A deployment that changes only a decorative detail does not justify repeatedly announcing the entire archive.

For a static site, the sequence I would implement is:

  1. Build the source and validate the generated HTML, sitemap, and feeds.
  2. Publish the approved commit to the production host.
  3. Wait until the changed public pages match the intended release.
  4. Submit the affected URL inventory to IndexNow.
  5. Save the response and review engine reporting later.

A successful API response records acceptance, not a completed crawl. A response awaiting key verification also needs follow up. Record the HTTP status alongside the host, time, and submitted count. If a request fails, inspect the cause before retrying; do not create an endless loop that hides a broken verification file.

Use Bing Webmaster Tools as a diagnostic instrument

Verify the business domain in Bing Webmaster Tools and review its sitemap and URL inspection information. Look at the exact production address when investigating a missing article. Keep old and new URLs together during a migration so a redirect can be evaluated against its intended destination.

A submission report and an index report answer different questions. If a URL was notified but remains unavailable in search, examine the content, access rules, canonical choice, and engine feedback. Repeated submissions do not fix an incorrect canonical or a page that needs authentication.

I would also retain the existing Google Search Console routine. IndexNow's participant list does not currently include Google. Use the site's Google reports to assess Google discovery and indexing rather than infer success from a Bing notification.

Give the Guides a feed that another site can actually use

A summary feed is enough for a headline widget. Republishing a Guide needs more: article content, a stable identifier, a source link, reliable dates, and absolute links inside the imported body. A relative image or navigation address that works on the originating website may point somewhere else after import.

The Gerris Guides RSS feed carries full article content, and the Atom version provides an alternative. An importer should preserve the original source URL and recognize the same identifier on subsequent runs. Test one article in Plone before enabling automatic ingestion for the whole archive.

Decide whether the destination displays excerpts or republishes complete articles. A full copy deserves visible attribution and a deliberate canonical policy. A feed cannot control the metadata that a separate CMS emits. Check the resulting Plone page, including its links and images, rather than assume feed parsing completed the SEO work.

Measure the business result independently

For each release, retain a short note of the question it answers, the production URL, the publication date, and the intended reader. Review search visibility and referred traffic against that record. If you test assistant answers, keep the question wording and the linked sources so another person can inspect the observation.

The strongest operational outcome is a process that can distinguish publication failure from indexing delay and editorial weakness. Those require different remedies. Start with one useful Guide, establish the checkpoints, then repeat the process for the next article. For broader release planning, the website migration checklist shows how inventories and verification fit together.

item.content:encoded:
Repositories plus super intelligence: the SEO superpower nobody told you to learn

By Chris Abraham · Published October 11, 2026

On September 29, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order replacing "Artificial Intelligence" with "Super Intelligence" across the executive branch. Call it AI, SI, or a very fast intern; for anyone in SEO, the name matters less than what it does when you pair it with the other half of the equation: the code repository. Git plus a capable coding assistant is a real superpower. It takes you far outside the confines of being a Yoast monkey or a Screaming Frog jockey.

Half one: the repository

Every serious website now lives in version control, almost always Git, which Linus Torvalds and the Linux kernel community built in 2005 after losing free use of their previous tool. Before Git, teams used CVS and then Subversion. Today the code sits on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket, and every change arrives as a commit, gets proposed as a pull request, is reviewed, and can be rolled back.

For SEO, that means the things you care about are files. Title patterns, canonical logic, hreflang, structured data, redirects, robots rules, sitemaps, internal linking modules, and lazy loading behavior are all written down somewhere in the repository. If you can't read it, you're guessing about it from the outside.

Half two: super intelligence that reads code

Coding assistants have moved past autocomplete. GitHub says Copilot can now answer questions about a repository, plan and make changes, run tests in a cloud environment, and review pull requests. Anthropic's Claude Code does the same from a terminal, and OpenAI offers Codex alongside ChatGPT. Point one at a codebase and ask where the canonical tag comes from, and it will find the component, the function feeding it, and the edge case that breaks it, in minutes.

Why each half fails alone

  • A repository without AI is a wall of unfamiliar code. Most SEOs never get past the folder list, so they file a ticket and wait.
  • AI without a repository is copy and paste from a chat window: snippets with no history, no review, and no way to know whether the fix ever shipped or what else it broke.
  • Together, the assistant reads and drafts, Git records and protects, and the SEO supplies the one thing neither has: knowing what search engines and AI answer engines actually need.

What the superpower looks like in practice

  • Diagnosis down to the line. A crawl tells you product pages render 300 words. The repository tells you a scroll triggered component never mounts for a crawler. I found exactly that once, and it's the difference between "Google doesn't like the page" and a fix a developer can ship the same day. The details are in my JavaScript SEO guide.
  • Migrations with receipts. Redirect maps written as config, tested against the old URL list before launch, and reviewed like any other code.
  • Fixes at template scale. One pull request repairs every page built from that template, today and in the future.
  • Your own tools. I direct Claude Code like a small development team; it has built me a command line assistant with a full test suite, moved a legacy blog off dead software, and built this website. See what I built with Claude Code.

How to start, if you're an SEO

  1. Learn six Git words: clone, branch, commit, diff, pull request, merge. That's enough to be useful and safe.
  2. Ask for read access to a client's repository. Read only is an easy yes for most teams.
  3. Have the assistant give you the tour. Ask it to explain the structure, where templates live, and where every SEO element is generated.
  4. Make your first pull request tiny, such as a title pattern or a missing canonical, and let the developer review it.
  5. Write the rules down in a project memory file and turn them into automated checks, so the assistant follows them every time.
  6. Check everything. The assistant is confidently wrong often enough that verification is the job. My method for doing this safely is in how to use AI coding assistants on a business website.

What this means for your business

If you run a company with a website, the question to ask your SEO is no longer whether they know the plugin. It's whether they can read the code and send a pull request. An SEO with both halves of the superpower costs you fewer developer hours, finds the cause, and leaves a reviewed history of every change.

Hire the superpower

This is how I work every day: in the repository, through pull requests, with super intelligence doing the heavy reading under my direction and my name on the result. I can be your fractional technical lead, turn a diagnosis into developer ready specs and verify they shipped, or build you small AI tools safely. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you what the code is doing to your search visibility.

SEO 101: a first principles primer for any website

By Chris Abraham · Published October 9, 2026

Search engine optimization sounds like a dark art. It's mostly common sense, applied carefully. A search engine has one job: send each searcher to the page that best answers the question. Everything in SEO follows from helping it do that job, and from never trying to fool it. This primer works for any website on any platform, from a hand-coded page to a store with ten thousand products.

Principle 1: understand the machine

Search works in three stages.

  1. Crawling. Programs called crawlers follow links from page to page and download what they find.
  2. Indexing. The engine reads each page, figures out what it's about, and files it in an enormous catalog.
  3. Serving. When someone searches, the engine pulls the most useful pages from that catalog and ranks them.

AI answers in Google, Bing, and ChatGPT search draw on the same kind of catalog. A page that can't be crawled can't be indexed, and a page that isn't indexed can't be ranked or quoted by anyone. That is why the technical basics come first.

Principle 2: write for people first

Google's own guidance asks one question of every page: was it made to help a person, or to attract search traffic? Write the page you'd want to find. Answer the question fully, in plain language, early on the page. Include what only you know: your prices, your process, your photos, your results. A page that would read the same with any company's name swapped in gives a searcher nothing new.

Principle 3: earn trust with E-E-A-T

Google's search quality raters judge pages for experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness, and Google describes trust as the most important of the four. You show them on the page itself:

  • Experience: evidence you've actually done the thing, such as real photos, real numbers, and lessons learned the hard way.
  • Expertise: a named author with a short bio and the credentials that matter for the topic.
  • Authoritativeness: other respected people and sites mentioning and linking to you.
  • Trust: accurate content, a real address and contact details, clear policies, HTTPS, and sources for your claims.

Principle 4: label every page clearly

  • Title tag: the clickable headline in search results. Make it unique, specific, and about 50 to 60 characters, with the page's main subject near the front.
  • Meta description: the summary under the headline. A clear 140 to 160 character description earns the click, even though it plays no direct part in ranking.
  • One H1: a single main heading that says what the page is about, followed by H2 and H3 subheadings in order, like an outline.
  • Readable URLs: /services/roof-repair/ tells people and crawlers more than /page?id=4817.

Principle 5: link with words that mean something

Internal links, from one page of your site to another, are how crawlers find your pages and how they learn what each page covers. The clickable words matter. "Read more," "click here," and "learn more" tell nobody anything, and a screen reader user who pulls up a list of a page's links hears the same useless phrase ten times. Make the link text describe the destination, the way "see my guide to Core Web Vitals" names exactly where the click leads. Link from strong pages to the pages you most want found, and make sure every important page is reachable through ordinary links, without relying on search boxes or scripts.

Principle 6: describe every meaningful image

Alt text is the written description of an image, read aloud by screen readers and read by search engines. Describe what the picture shows in a short sentence, and include any words that appear in it. Skip "image of" and "photo of"; screen readers already announce that it's an image. Decorative images, such as background flourishes, get an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip them. Keyword lists in alt text help nobody and look like spam.

Principle 7: make it fast and stable

Google's Core Web Vitals measure three things: how fast the main content appears (Largest Contentful Paint, good under 2.5 seconds), how quickly the page responds to a tap or click (Interaction to Next Paint, good under 200 milliseconds), and whether the layout jumps around while loading (Cumulative Layout Shift, good under 0.1). Compress and correctly size images, load fewer scripts, and give images width and height so the page doesn't shift. Test any page free in PageSpeed Insights. For the details, see my Core Web Vitals guide.

Principle 8: build it so everyone can use it

Accessibility and SEO want the same things: real text, logical headings, descriptive links, alt text, captions, enough color contrast, and a site that works with a keyboard alone. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are the standard, and in the United States the ADA has been applied to websites in court. Every accessibility fix makes the site easier to crawl too. See ADA website compliance and testing a site in a text browser.

My standing recommendation: put the site behind Cloudflare

For almost every site, I recommend running DNS and caching through Cloudflare. Even its free plan speeds up pages, handles HTTPS certificates, and absorbs attacks, and it sells domains at cost. Hosted builders such as Shopify, Squarespace, and Wix are the exception; with those, keep Cloudflare to DNS only. My Cloudflare guide covers which plan to choose, what to budget, and the settings that help or hurt search.

Principle 9: open the door for crawlers

  • Keep robots.txt from blocking pages you want found.
  • Publish an XML sitemap listing your important pages, and submit it in Google Search Console. Then open Bing Webmaster Tools and use its import option to copy every verified site and sitemap over from Search Console in a few clicks. Both tools are free, and I check both regularly to make sure the sitemaps are read without errors.
  • Turn on IndexNow, through Cloudflare, your SEO plugin, or your platform, so Bing and other participating engines hear about new and changed pages right away.
  • Use HTTPS everywhere, and pick one version of the domain, with or without www, and redirect the other to it.
  • Add structured data that matches what the page visibly says.

Principle 10: stay white hat

Every shortcut on this list has hurt real businesses, some permanently: buying links, keyword stuffing, hidden text, pages written only to rank, mass AI content nobody reviewed, fake reviews, and fake authors. The search engines publish their spam policies openly. Read them once, and you'll recognize the pitches in your inbox for what they are.

Your first week

  1. Verify the site in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, and submit the sitemap.
  2. List your ten most important pages, and give each a unique title, description, and H1.
  3. Replace every "read more" and "click here" with descriptive link text.
  4. Add alt text to every meaningful image.
  5. Run your home page and one inner page through PageSpeed Insights, and fix the largest problem it names.
  6. Ask three happy customers for reviews on your Google Business Profile.

  • How Google writes title links and how it writes snippets

item.title: Ranking yourself first in a "best of" list now backfires in AI answers
item.description: How self ranked best agency lists came to steer AI answers, why Google, Anthropic, and the data now push back, and what earns a real AI recommendation instead.
item.content:encoded:
Ranking yourself first in a "best of" list now backfires in AI answers

By Chris Abraham · Published October 9, 2026

Ask ChatGPT, Gemini, or Google's AI Mode for the best AI search agency and you get a confident shortlist. Look at where that shortlist comes from and you find something funny: most of the sources are "best agency" lists written by agencies that put themselves first. For about two years that trick worked. In 2026 the search engines, the AI companies, and the data all turned against it at once.

How the trick works

AI assistants assemble recommendations from pages that already compare options, and a list titled "best GEO agencies in 2026" is exactly that kind of page. So agencies publish one, rank themselves first, and fill the rest with respectable competitors so the list looks fair. A few are candid about it. One list opens with its author admitting the self-ranking in a single word: "Guilty." Others score themselves highest on a scoring system they designed. The pattern is easy to spot in the search results for any "best agency" query this month.

One agency studied the effect from the inside. Tracking 48 AI answers to four "which agency" prompts in late summer 2026, it found that almost every frequently cited source was an agency's own list ranking itself first, and that a single agency's site supplied the source for 14 of the 48 answers. Its conclusion, in its own words: the agencies AI recommends are, to a large degree, the agencies that published the lists AI reads. That agency then published its own scored list, and kept itself out of the ranking.

Why it stopped working

  • Google changed the rules in May. Its spam policies now open by including attempts to manipulate generative AI responses in Search. Lists built mainly to plant a recommendation sit squarely in that territory, alongside hidden instructions and fake sources.
  • The citations are already falling. Lily Ray tracked 100 "best B2B software" queries in Google's AI Overviews. Compared with June, September's answers cited 38 percent fewer self-promotional "best of" lists, and the brand that published the list was left out of the recommendation 83 percent of the time, up from 69 percent. One researcher and one sample, but the direction is clear.
  • The AI companies are closing the door too. Anthropic's updated usage policy, released October 8 and effective November 12, forbids using Claude to manipulate the sources search engines and AI systems draw answers from by seeding content that misrepresents its origin, authorship, or independence. Its example: networks of sites posing as unaffiliated sources that corroborate the same claims.

When the engine, the referee, and the tool maker all move in the same direction, the tactic has a short future.

What earns a real recommendation

Assistants are trying to do what a careful buyer does: find independent evidence that several unrelated people reached the same conclusion. Give them that evidence.

  • Reviews on platforms you don't control: Google Business Profile, Clutch, G2, and the directories of your industry.
  • Lists written by someone else: trade press, analysts, associations, and customers' own write-ups.
  • Case studies with checkable detail: a named client where permitted, dates, before and after figures, and the method.
  • Honest comparison pages: if you compare yourself with competitors, say so plainly, state who each option suits, and include the ones that beat you on something.
  • A consistent entity: the same name, description, people, and profiles everywhere, so every system recognizes one business.

If you already published a self-ranked list

Disclose the authorship at the top in a sentence a reader can't miss, publish the scoring method, and score yourself by the same rules as everyone else, or step out of the ranking entirely. Better still, turn it into a buyer's checklist that helps people choose well, with your own offer described once, at the end, as one option.

How to vet anyone selling AI visibility

  1. Show me an AI answer that names one of your clients, with the date.
  2. Which tool measures it, and can I see the raw prompts?
  3. What do you do off my site, and do any of those placements hide who paid for them?
  4. Do you publish "best of" lists that rank your own firm, or place clients in them?
  5. Which of your tactics would you stop doing if Google or Anthropic wrote about them tomorrow?

Every answer to the last question tells you how long the results will last. For the wider picture, see the state of search in 2026 and how AI assistants decide what to say about your business, or ask me what the assistants say about yours.
